summary: The main difference between jaguars and leopards is geography and build: jaguars live in the Americas and are stockier, with a broader head and a more powerful bite, while leopards live in Africa and Asia and are slimmer and longer-tailed. Both have rosettes, but a jaguar's are larger and usually have one or more small spots inside them.

differences.title: Range
differences.text: The two never meet in the wild. Jaguars are the only big cats of the Americas, ranging from northern Mexico through Central America to northern Argentina, with their stronghold in the Amazon basin and the Pantanal. Leopards have the widest range of any big cat, across sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and much of Asia.

differences.title: Rosettes
differences.text: Both cats are covered in rosettes, but the patterns differ. A jaguar's rosettes are large, bold and widely spaced, and most enclose one or more small black dots. A leopard's rosettes are smaller, more numerous and packed closer together, and their centers are empty, showing only slightly darker fur.

differences.title: Build
differences.text: The jaguar is the heavier, more compact cat, with a barrel chest, short sturdy legs, a noticeably broad head and a relatively short tail. The leopard is lighter and more elongated, with a smaller head and a long tail that helps it balance in trees. Jaguars are the third-largest cat, after tigers and lions.

differences.title: Bite and killing method
differences.text: Relative to its size, the jaguar has the strongest bite of any big cat. It often kills by biting straight through the skull or the back of the neck, and it can pierce turtle shells and caiman hide. Leopards, like most big cats, usually kill by clamping the throat until the prey suffocates.

differences.title: Water and trees
differences.text: Jaguars love water. They swim readily, patrol riverbanks and hunt caimans, capybaras and fish. Leopards can swim but mostly avoid it. They are the better climbers and famously haul heavy kills into trees to keep them from lions and hyenas, a habit jaguars rarely need because they have no such competitors.

differences.title: Conservation status
differences.text: The jaguar is listed as Near Threatened and has lost roughly half of its historical range, including nearly all of it in the United States. The leopard is listed as Vulnerable. Although still widespread, leopards have vanished from large parts of Asia and North Africa, and several subspecies, such as the Amur leopard, are Critically Endangered.

similarities: Jaguars and leopards are both members of the genus Panthera and can roar, giving a hoarse, repetitive sawing call. Both are solitary, territorial ambush hunters that are active mainly at dusk and at night, and both take a very wide variety of prey. Both also produce black individuals through melanism. These so-called black panthers still show rosettes in good light.
howToTell: Check the rosettes for spots inside. Dots within the rings mean jaguar; empty rings mean leopard.
A heavy, broad-headed, short-tailed cat is a jaguar. A sleeker cat with a long tail is a leopard.
Location settles it for wild animals: the Americas mean jaguar, while Africa or Asia means leopard.
A spotted big cat swimming or hunting along a river is more likely a jaguar.

faq.question: Who would win a fight, a jaguar or a leopard?
faq.answer: A jaguar would probably win, since it is heavier, more muscular and has a considerably stronger bite. This is purely hypothetical, because the two species live on different continents and never meet. Both cats normally avoid fights with other large predators, because an injury can be fatal.

faq.question: Is a black panther a jaguar or a leopard?
faq.answer: It can be either. 'Black panther' is not a species but a name for any big cat with a black coat caused by melanism. In Africa and Asia it is a black leopard, and in the Americas it is a black jaguar. The spots remain faintly visible.

faq.question: Can jaguars and leopards interbreed?
faq.answer: Yes, in captivity. The two are closely related, and zoos have produced hybrids, sometimes called jagupards or leguars, in the past. Hybrids never occur in nature, since the species are separated by oceans, and responsible modern zoos do not breed them.

faq.question: Which is bigger, a jaguar or a leopard?
faq.answer: The jaguar is bigger. It is the largest cat in the Americas and the third-largest in the world, and it is both heavier and more solidly built than a leopard. Size varies by region, and the largest jaguars live in Brazil's Pantanal wetlands.
